sections.h2: How a New York tax foreclosure or lien sale works
sections.html:
When property tax goes unpaid, a lien attaches and the owner gets a fixed period to pay it off. If the period ends without payment, the tax district can foreclose in court, and in some places it can also sell the lien to an investor. Real Property Tax Law Article 11 sets out these procedures for the tax districts that follow it, and a few counties and cities enforce under their own charters instead.

The article is organized into titles: redemption, foreclosure by proceeding in rem, a homeowner bill of rights, general provisions, sales of delinquent tax liens, and distribution of surplus. A tax district that uses the article can end up with title through a court judgment, which is why the dates in your notice matter.

A private sale before that judgment lets you keep any equity above the tax debt.

sections.h2: How long you have to redeem
sections.html:
The redemption period ends two years after the lien date. Under section 1110, you redeem by paying the enforcing officer the delinquent tax lien plus all legal charges on or before the last day.

  • A tax district can lengthen the period for residential or farm property to three or four years by local law, under section 1111.
  • A tax district can shorten it to one year for residential vacant and abandoned property that was placed on a vacant and abandoned roll or list before the taxes became delinquent.
  • If the published foreclosure notice names a later date, the redemption period runs to that later date.

The statute defines residential property as a one-, two- or three-family structure used only for residential purposes. Ask your county treasurer or city finance office which period applies in your municipality and what date they show for your parcel.

sections.h2: What charges are added to the unpaid tax?
sections.html:
Legal charges are part of the delinquent tax, so they count toward the redemption amount. Section 1102 lists them: costs of mailing and publishing notices, interest and penalties, recording fees, the cost of appraising the parcel to measure any surplus, and costs of searching the public record and other reasonable foreclosure expenses.

For that last group, the statute treats a charge of up to $250 per parcel, or 2% of the taxes, interest and penalties, whichever is greater, as reasonable without further proof. A tax district can charge more if it shows the court the larger amount was needed. When an officer posts a notice on the property itself, a $100 charge is added to the parcel under section 1125.

The enforcing officer must mail a notice of the foreclosure to each owner and to others whose interest appears in the public record, by both certified mail and first class mail. Under section 1125, the notice is treated as received unless both mailings come back within 45 days.

The notice warns that foreclosure will cost the owner the property and all rights in it, and states the last day to redeem. For a residential parcel, it comes with the homeowner warning notice from section 1144. That warning tells you:

  • You are at risk of losing your home, and you can call the Attorney General's Homeowner Protection Program hotline for free housing counseling or legal help.
  • If nothing is done within ninety days of the mailing, the tax district may start legal action.
  • You may remain in the home until a court orders you out, and the notice is not an eviction notice.
  • Seniors, people with physical disabilities and military service may qualify for a partial exemption, and the local assessor's office has the details.

Section 1125 also puts a duty on you: if your address changes, tell the enforcing officer in writing, since a court can weigh your failure to do so if you later claim you got no notice.

If you answer the petition and the court finds the answer has merit, the petition is dismissed for that parcel. If no answer is filed, the court awards possession to the tax district, and the enforcing officer deeds the property to the district or, if the officer asks and the court agrees, directly to another party. Once the deed is signed, every person who held a right, title, lien or equity of redemption in the parcel is barred from asserting it.

When the court orders a sale after an answer, the officer holds a public auction after notice runs once a week for at least three successive weeks in a local newspaper. Section 1136 also lets the tax district, before the parcel is conveyed to a third party, convey title back to the former owner on payment of the taxes, penalties, interest and other lawful charges, but that is the district's choice.

sections.h2: Getting money back if the property sells high
sections.html:
Possibly. Section 1197 allows anyone who held a right, title, interest, lien or equity of redemption just before the foreclosure judgment to file a claim with the court for a share of surplus from a sale.

The statute limits those claims. Where the property sold at public sale, the price paid is accepted as full value. For residential property, if no former homeowner has filed by the time the report of sale is confirmed and surplus remains, the proceeding stays open for at least three years. After that, unclaimed surplus is treated as abandoned and goes to the tax district to reduce its levy, not to the state comptroller.

In a lien sale, the tax district sells the debt rather than the house. Section 1190 allows a district to contract to sell some or all of its delinquent liens to the state's municipal bond bank or to tax lien entities the bank creates.

The enforcing officer must mail a notice at least 30 days before the sale to the owner and to anyone with a declaration of interest on file. After the sale, the buyer of the lien holds the right to collect, may hire a collection agency, and can take partial payments or set up installment agreements. You then pay the purchaser, not the municipality. Payments are applied first to collection costs and attorneys' fees, then to accrued interest, and last to principal.

Nassau County on Long Island shows how the calendar works. The Treasurer's Tax Records department collects delinquent county taxes, and for the towns of Hempstead, North Hempstead and Oyster Bay that includes both general and school taxes. Collection of unpaid school tax begins June 1 and general tax September 1 each year.

For the 2026 delinquent taxes, personal checks are taken from June 1 to November 30, 2026, and credit card or electronic check payments from June 26, 2026 to January 31, 2027. The last day to pay before the lien sale is Wednesday, February 10, 2027 at 3:00 PM. Tax liens themselves cannot be paid online and need a bank cashier's check or cash, and checks are made out to the Nassau County Treasurer, whose office is at 1 West Street in Mineola.

Other counties and cities run their own schedules. Ask your county treasurer, city finance office or receiver of taxes for the lien date, the redemption deadline and a written payoff figure.

sections.h2: Should you sell before the tax district acts?
sections.html:
Often, because a sale before the redemption date pays the taxes from the proceeds and leaves you whatever remains. After a judgment, your claim shrinks to a share of surplus that the court has to adjudicate.

Start by asking the enforcing officer for the full amount needed to redeem, including legal charges, and the exact last day. If the house is occupied by a tenant or full of an inherited estate's belongings, a buyer who purchases as-is can move faster than a listed sale. Get any payoff in writing and give it to the closing attorney so the lien is satisfied at the table.

faqs.q: How long is the redemption period in New York?
faqs.a: Two years after the lien date under Real Property Tax Law section 1110. A tax district may extend it to three or four years for residential or farm property, or cut it to one year for vacant and abandoned residential property.

faqs.q: Do I lose my house the day the redemption period ends?
faqs.a: No. After the period ends the tax district must still win a court judgment, and the notice you receive says you can stay until a court orders you to leave. The notice states the last date to redeem.

faqs.q: Can I get the extra money if my house sells for more than I owe?
faqs.a: Yes, you can file a claim under section 1197 for a share of surplus. For residential property, the proceeding stays open at least three years after the sale report is confirmed if no former homeowner has filed.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a tax lien sale and a tax foreclosure?
faqs.a: A lien sale transfers the right to collect the debt to a purchaser, and you keep the house while you owe the purchaser. A foreclosure ends with a court judgment that transfers ownership of the property to the tax district or its grantee.

faqs.q: Who can I call for free help with property tax arrears?
faqs.a: The homeowner warning notice lists the Attorney General's Homeowner Protection Program hotline, 1-855-HOME-456, and housing counseling agencies in your county. You can also ask your enforcing officer about a payment plan.
